Modals of Necessity: Must/Have to/Have got to
You use the modals must, have to and have got to talk about necessity.
Must is the strongest of these three modal verbs. It is most common in writing and rarely used in questions. You can use it to talk about the present and the future.
I feel like it's something I must do.
Have got to is the most common in casual conversations. It is not used in questions. You use it to talk about present and future obligations.
Is there anything you've got to do to prepare?
Have to is the most common. You use it to form questions and negatives. You can use it on all tenses (past, present and future).
I have to be in the trenches, you know?
You don't have to go all the way to Lesotho to do that.
I mustn't leave anything to chance.

images.text:
Vanessa: What's this I hear about you traveling to Lesotho?
Amy: It's true, provided that I can get all my travel documents in order, I'll be leaving at the end of the month.
Vanessa: What prompted you to make such a life-altering decision?
Amy: Well, after a great deal of soul-searching I decided that I'm just not cut out for this behind the scenes stuff. I have to be in the trenches, you know?
Vanessa: What will you do there?

Amy: I'm going so that I can lend a hand. It's that simple.
Vanessa: But you don't have to go all the way to Lesotho to do that. You're definitely lending a hand, whether you do it from home or abroad.
Amy: That's true, but in order that the project is completed on time we need people on the ground. I think that I have the ability to convey a sense of urgency to the project managers. It's a matter of life and death, after all.
Vanessa: As always your passion is really inspiring, Amy.

Amy: It's really become a pet project of mine. More than that, even, I feel like it's something I must do.
Vanessa: Is there anything you've got to do to prepare?
Amy: Yeah, I've got to renew my passport, and if I want to cross over into South Africa, I'll have to get a special visa.
Vanessa: Not to mention shots and pills, lest you catch malaria or something.
Amy: Of course, I mustn't leave anything to chance.
